definitions.text: To loose, or release, from, or as from, a cage.
Not called for; not required or needed; improper; gratuitous; wanton.
To disturb; to disquiet. Dryden.
To break up the camp of; to dislodge from camp. [R.] If they could but now uncamp their enemies. Milton.
Not canny; unsafe; strange; weird; ghostly. Sir W. Scott.
To deprive of canonical authority.
To reduce from the rank of a canonized saint.
To remove a cap or cover from.
Incapable. [Obs.] "Uncapable of conviction." Locke.
To remove a cap or cape from. [Obs.]
An instrument for removing an explode cap from a cartridge shell.
To degrade from the cardinalship.
Not cared for; not heeded; -- with for.
Not fleshy; specifically, not made flesh; not incarnate. [R.] Sir T. Browne.
To divest of flesh.
To take from, or set free from, a cart; to unload.
To take out of a case or covering; to remove a case or covering from; to uncover. L'Estrange.
To strip; to flay. [Obs.]
(Mil.)
To display, or spread to view, as a flag, or the colors of a military body.
To take a castle from; to turn out of a castle.
Having no antecedent cause; uncreated; self-existent; eternal. A. Baxter.
Incautious. [Obs.]
Incautious.
Incautiously.
A claw. [Obs.]
An ounce; a small portion. [Obs.] "By unces hung his locks." Chaucer.
Not capable of being ended; unceasing. [R.]
To throw from its center.
To throw from its center.
To remove from its actual century. [R.] It has first to uncentury itself. H. Drummond.
Not certain; not having certain knowledge; not assured in mind; distrustful. Chaucer. Man, without the protection of a superior Being, . . . is uncertain of everything that he hopes for. Tillotson.
Irresolute; inconsonant; variable; untrustworthy; as, an uncertain person; an uncertain breeze. O woman! in our hours of ease, Uncertain, coy, and hard to please! Sir W. Scott.
Questionable; equivocal; indefinite; problematical. "The fashion of uncertain evils." Milton. From certain dangers to uncertain praise. Dryden.
Not sure; liable to fall or err; fallible. Soon bent his bow, uncertain in his aim. Dryden. Whistling slings dismissed the uncertain stone. Gay.
To make uncertain. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.
In an uncertain manner.
The quality or state of being uncertain.
That which is uncertain; something unknown. Our shepherd's case is every man's case that quits a moral certainty for an uncertainty. L'Estrange.
Incessant. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.
To free from chains or slavery; to let loose. Prior.
Happening at a bad time; unseasonable; inconvenient. A. Trollope.
Ill-fated; unlucky. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
Unsafe to meddle with; dangerous. [Scot.]
To remove from a chaplaincy.
To free from a charge or load; to unload. Wyclif.
To free from an accusation; to make no charge against; to acquit. Shak.
To throw out of a chariot. Pope.
Not charitable; contrary to charity; severe in judging; harsh; censorious; as, uncharitable opinions or zeal. Addison.
Uncharitableness. Tennyson. 'T were much uncharity in you. J. Webster.
To release from a charm, fascination, or secret power; to disenchant. Beau. & Fl.
To remove from a charnel house; to raise from the grave; to exhume. Byron.
Not chaste; not continent; lewd.
The quality or state of being unchaste; lewdness; incontinence.
Not capable of being checked or stopped. [R.]
To bereave of children; to make childless. Shak.
To make unlike a child; to divest of the characteristics of a child. Bp. Hall.
To render unchristian. [Obs. & R.] Milton.
Not christened; as, an unchristened child.
Not Christian; not converted to the Christian faith; infidel.
Contrary to Christianity; not like or becoming a Christian; as, unchristian conduct.
To make unchristian. [Obs.] South.
To turn from the Christian faith; to cause to abandon the belief and profession of Christianity.
Unchristian. Milton.
In an unchristian manner.
The quality or state of being unchristian. [R.] Eikon Basilike.
To expel, or cause to separate, from a church; to excommunicate. Sir M. Hale.
To deprive of the character, privileges, and authority of a church. South.
(Rom. Antiq.)
A twelfth part, as of the Roman as; an ounce.
(Alg.)
A numerical coefficient in any particular case of the binomial theorem. [Obs.]

Of, pertaining to, or designating, a certain style of letters used in ancient manuscripts, esp. in Greek and Latin manuscripts. The letters are somewhat rounded, and the upstrokes and downstrokes usually have a slight inclination. These letters were used as early as the 1st century b. c., and were seldom used after the 10th century a. d., being superseded by the cursive style.
An uncial letter.
Ounce by ounce.
Having the shape of a hook; being of a curved or hooked from; hooklike. Unciform bone (Anat.), a bone of the carpus at the bases of the fourth and fifth metacarpals; the hamatum.
The unciform bone. See Illust. of Perissodactyla.
A division of marine chætopod annelids which are furnished with uncini, as the serpulas and sabellas.
Hooked; bent at the tip in the form of a hook; as, an uncinate process.
The unciform bone.
One of the peculiar minute chitinous hooks found in large numbers in the tori of tubicolous annelids belonging to the Uncinata.
To decipher; as, to uncipher a letter. [Obs.] Sir W. Temple.
Not circumcised; hence, not of the Israelites. "This uncircumcised Philistine." 1 Sam. xvii. 26.
The absence or want of circumcision.
(Script.)
People not circumcised; the Gentiles.
Not circumstantial; not entering into minute particulars.
Not important; not pertinent; trivial. [Obs.]
To deprive of the rank or rights of a city. [Obs.]
Not civilized; savage; barbarous; uncivilized. Men can not enjoy the rights of an uncivil and of a civil state together. Burke.
Not civil; not complaisant; discourteous; impolite; rude; unpolished; as, uncivil behavior.
Incivility. [Obs.]
The state of being uncivilized; savagery or barbarism. [R.]
Not civilized; not reclaimed from savage life; rude; barbarous; savage; as, the uncivilized inhabitants of Central Africa.
Not civil; coarse; clownish. [R.] Addison.
In an uncivil manner.
To loose the clasp of; to open, as something that is fastened, or as with, a clasp; as, to unclasp a book; to unclasp one's heart.
The brother of one's father or mother; also applied to an aunt's husband; -- the correlative of aunt in sex, and of nephew and niece in relationship.
A pawnbroker. [Slang] Thackeray. My uncle, a pawnbroker. [Slang] - - Uncle Sam, a humorous appellation given to the United States Government. See Uncle Sam, in Dictionary of Noted Names in Fiction.
Not clean; foul; dirty; filthy.
Ceremonially impure; needing ritual cleansing. He that toucheth the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days. Num. xix. 11.
Morally impure. "Adultery of the heart, consisting of inordinate and unclean affections." Perkins. Israelites were forbidden to use for food.
Incapable of being cleansed or cleaned.
Same as Unclinch.
The office or position of an uncle. Lamb.
To unwind, unfold, or untie; hence, to undo; to ruin. Shak.
To cause to be no longer clinched; to open; as, to unclinch the fist. [Written also unclench.]
To cease from clinging or adhering. [Obs.] Milton.
To remove a cloak or cover from; to deprive of a cloak or cover; to unmask; to reveal.
To remove, or take off, one's cloak.
To disencumber of a clog, or of difficulties and obstructions; to free from encumbrances; to set at liberty. Shak.
To release from a cloister, or from confinement or seclusion; to set free; to liberate.
To open; to separate the parts of; as, to unclose a letter; to unclose one's eyes.
To disclose; to lay open; to reveal.
Not separated by inclosures; open. Clarendon.
Not finished; not concluded. [R.] Madison.
Not closed; not sealed; open. Byron.
To strip of clothes or covering; to make naked. I. Watts. [We] do groan being burdened; not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon. 2 Cor. v. 4.
Etym: [Properly p. p. of unclothe.]
Divested or stripped of clothing. Byron.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + clothed.]
Not yet clothed; wanting clothes; naked.
To free from clouds; to unvail; to clear from obscurity, gloom, sorrow, or the like. Beau. & Fl.
To unwind; to untangle.
To open, as something closely shut. "Unclutch his griping hand." Dr. H. More.
(Mech.)
To disengage, as a clutch.
Unknown; strange, or foreign; unusual, or surprising; distant in manner; reserved. [Scot.]
In a high degree; to a great extent; greatly; very. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
A strange thing or person. [Scot.]
To detach or loose from a coach. [Obs.] Chapman.
To let down the cock of, as a firearm.
To deprive of its cocked shape, as a hat, etc.
To open or spread from a cock or heap, as hay.
To release from a coffle.
To deprive of the coif or cap. Young.
To unwind or open, as a coil of rope. Derham.
Not coined, or minted; as, uncoined silver. Locke.
Not fabricated; not artificial or counterfeit; natural. "Plain and uncoined constancy." Shak.
To unhorse. [Obs. & R.] Shak.
To separate, as substances in combination; to release from combination or union. [R.] Daniel.
Not to be come at, or reached; inaccessible. [Colloq.] Addison. My honor is infallible and uncomeatable. Congreve.
Not comely.
Feeling discomfort; uneasy; as, to be uncomfortable on account of one's position.
Causing discomfort; disagreeable; unpleasant; as, an uncomfortable seat or situation. The most dead, uncomfortable time of the year. Addison.
Not common; unusual; infrequent; rare; hence, remarkable; strange; as, an uncommon season; an uncommon degree of cold or heat; uncommon courage.
Incomplete. Pope.
To fail to comprehend. [R.] Daniel.
Unable to comprehend. Narrow-spirited, uncomprehensive zealots. South.
Incomprehensible. [Obs.] Shak.
Not admitting of compromise; making no truce or concessions; obstinate; unyielding; inflexible.
Inconceivable. [Obs.] Locke.
Want of concern; absence of anxiety; freedom from solicitude; indifference. A listless unconcern, Cold, and averting from our neighbor's good. Thomson.

Not concerned; not anxious or solicitous; easy in mind; carelessly secure; indifferent; as, to be unconcerned at what has happened; to be unconcerned about the future. Happy mortals, unconcerned for more. Dryden.
Not interesting of affecting; insignificant; not belonging to one. [Obs.] Addison.
The state of being unconcerned, or of having no share or concern; unconcernedness. [Obs.] South.
Inconclusive. [Obs.] Locke.
Inconclusive. [Obs.] Locke.
Inconclusive. [Obs.]

Not conditional limited, or conditioned; made without condition; absolute; unreserved; as, an unconditional surrender. O, pass not, Lord, an absolute decree, Or bind thy sentence unconditional. Dryden.
Not conditioned or subject to conditions; unconditional.
(Metaph.)

Not subject to condition or limitations; infinite; absolute; hence, inconceivable; incogitable. Sir W. Hamilton. The unconditioned (Metaph.), all that which is inconceivable and beyond the realm of reason; whatever is inconceivable under logical forms or relations.
Absence of confidence; uncertainty; doubt.
Unlike. [Obs.] Not unconform to other shining globes. Milton.
The quality or state of being unconformable; unconformableness.
(Geol.)
Want of parallelism between one series of strata and another, especially when due to a disturbance of the position of the earlier strata before the latter were deposited.
Not conformable; not agreeable; not conforming. Moral evil is an action unconformable to it [the rule of our duty]. I. Watts.
(Geol.)
Not conformable; not lying in a parallel position; as, unconformable strata.
A nonconformist. [Obs.]
Want of conformity; incongruity; inconsistency. South.
(Geol.)

Want of parallelism between strata in contact. unconformability; but it is often used more broadly, for example, to include the case when the parallelism of strata once conformable has been disturbed by faulting and the like.
To free from a state of confusion, or of being confounded. Milton.
Not confounded. Bp. Warburton.
To thaw; to become liquid again. Tennyson.
Not knowing; ignorant. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Ignorance. [Obs.]
Not conquerable; indomitable.

Not conscionable; not conforming to reason; unreasonable; exceeding the limits of any reasonable claim or expectation; inordinate; as, an unconscionable person or demand; unconscionable size. Which use of reason, most reasonless and unconscionable, is the utmost that any tyrant ever pretended. Milton. His giantship is gone somewhat crestfallen, Stalking with less unconscionable strides. Milton.
Not guided by, or conformed to, conscience. [Obs.] Ungenerous as well as unconscionable practices. South.
Not conscious; having no consciousness or power of mental perception; without cerebral appreciation; hence, not knowing or regarding; ignorant; as, an unconscious man. Cowper.
Not known or apprehended by consciousness; as, an unconscious cerebration. "Unconscious causes." Blackmore.
Having no knowledge by experience; -- followed by of; as, a mule unconscious of the yoke. Pope.
To render not sacred; to deprive of sanctity; to desecrate.
Inconsequential. Johnson.
Inconsiderate; heedless; careless. [Obs.] Daniel.
Not considered or attended to; not regarded; inconsiderable; trifling. A snapper-up of unconsidered trifles. Shak.
Incongruous; inconsistent. "A thing unconsonant.' Hooker.
Inconspicuous. [R.] Ed. Rev.
Inconstancy. [Obs.] "The unconstancy of the foundation." Fuller.
Not constant; inconstant; fickle; changeable. [Obs.] Shak.
Not constitutional; not according to, or consistent with, the terms of a constitution of government; contrary to the constitution; as, an unconstitutional law, or act of an officer. Burke.
Freedom from constraint; ease. Felton.
Not consummated; not accomplished. [Obs.] Dryden.
Incontestable.
Not continent; incontinent. Wyclif (2 Tim. iii. 3).
Incapable of being controlled; ungovernable; irresistible; as, an uncontrollable temper; uncontrollable events.
Indisputable; irrefragable; as, an uncontrollable maxim; an uncontrollable title. [R.] Swift.
Not involving controversy. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
Incontrovertible.
Incontrovertibly.
Inconvenient. Bale.
The state of being unconverted; impenitence. [R.]
Not converted or exchanged.
Not changed in opinion, or from one faith to another. Specifically: -- (a) Not persuaded of the truth of the Christian religion; heathenish. Hooker. (b) Unregenerate; sinful; impenitent. Baxter.
To release from cords; to loosen the cord or cords of; to unfasten or unbind; as, to uncord a package.
To draw the cork from; as, to uncork a bottle.
Incorrect. Dryden.
Incorrigible; not capable of correction. [Obs.]
Incorrupt.
Incorruptible. "The glory of the uncorruptible God." Rom. i. 23.
Incorruption.
To loose, as dogs, from their couples; also, to set loose; to disconnect; to disjoin; as, to uncouple railroad cars.
To roam at liberty. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Absence of courtliness; rudeness; rusticity. Addison.
Hooklike; hooked. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
Unknown. [Obs.] "This uncouth errand." Milton. To leave the good that I had in hand, In hope of better that was uncouth. Spenser.
Uncommon; rare; exquisite; elegant. [Obs.] Harness . . . so uncouth and so rish. Chaucer.

Unfamiliar; strange; hence, mysterious; dreadful; also, odd; awkward; boorish; as, uncouth manners. "Uncouth in guise and gesture." I. Taylor. I am surprised with an uncouth fear. Shak. Thus sang the uncouth swain. Milton.
Not covenable; inconvenient. [Obs.] Wyclif (1 Tim. iv. 7).
Not covenanted; not granted or entered into under a covenant, agreement, or contract. Bp. Horsley.

Not having joined in a league, or assented to a covenant or agreement, as to the Solemn League and Covenant of the Scottish people in the times of the Stuarts. In Scotland a few fanatical nonjurors may have grudged their allegiance to an uncovenanted king. Sir T. E. May.
(Theol.)
Not having entered into relationship with God through the appointed means of grace; also, not promised or assured by the divine promises or conditions; as, uncovenanted mercies.
To take the cover from; to divest of covering; as, to uncover a box, bed, house, or the like; to uncover one's body.
To show openly; to disclose; to reveal. "To uncover his perjury to the oath of his coronation." Milton.
To divest of the hat or cap; to bare the head of; as, to uncover one's head; to uncover one's self.
To take off the hat or cap; to bare the head in token of respect. We are forced to uncover after them. Addison.
To remove the covers from dishes, or the like. Uncover, dogs, and lap. Shak.
To divest or deprive of a cowl. Pope.
To deprive of existence; to annihilate. Who can uncreate thee, thou shalt know. Milton.
Uncreated; self-existent. Book of Common Prayer.
Deprived of existence; annihilated. Beau. & Fl.
Not yet created; as, misery uncreated. Milton.
Not existing by creation; self-existent; eternal; as, God is an uncreated being. Locke.
The quality or state of being uncreated.
Incredible. Bacon.
To cause to be disbelieved; to discredit. [Obs.] Fuller.
Discreditable. [Obs.]
To deprive of a crown; to take the crown from; hence, to discrown; to dethrone. He hath done me wrong, And therefore I'll uncrown him ere't be long. Shak.
Not cruddled, or curdled. [Obs.] Her breast like to a bowl of cream uncrudded. Spenser.

The act of anointing, smearing, or rubbing with an unguent, oil, or ointment, especially for medical purposes, or as a symbol of consecration; as, mercurial unction. To be heir, and to be king By sacred unction, thy deserved right. Milton.
That which is used for anointing; an unguent; an ointment; hence, anything soothing or lenitive. The king himself the sacred unction made. Dryden. Lay not that flattering unction to your soul. Shak.
Divine or sanctifying grace. [R.]

That quality in language, address, or the like, which excites emotion; especially, strong devotion; religious fervor and tenderness; sometimes, a simulated, factitious, or unnatural fervor. The delightful equivoque and unction of the passage in Farquhar. Hazlitt. The mention of thy glory Is unction to the breast. Neale (Rhythm of St. Bernard). Extreme unction (R. C. Ch. & Gr. Ch.), the sacrament of anointing in the last hours; the application of consecrated oil by a priest to all the senses, that is, to eyes, ears, nostrils, etc., of a person when in danger of death from illness, -- done for remission of sins. [James v. 14, 15.]
Unctuous. [Obs.]
Quality or state of being unctuous. Sir T. Browne.
Of the nature or quality of an unguent or ointment; fatty; oily; greasy. "The unctuous cheese." Longfellow.
Having a smooth, greasy feel, as certain minerals.
Bland; suave; also, tender; fervid; as, an unctuous speech; sometimes, insincerely suave or fervid.
Inculpable; not blameworthy. [R.] Hooker.
Not cultivated; rude; illiterate. [Obs.]
Want of culture. "Idleness, ill husbandry . . . unculture." Bp. Hall.
Ignorant. [Obs.] I am young and uncunning, as thou wost [knowest]. Chaucer.
Ignorantly. [Obs.]
Ignorance. [Obs.]
Incurable.
In an uncurable manner.
Not capable of being curbed. Shak.
To loose from curls, or ringlets; to straighten out, as anything curled or curly. He sheaths his paw, uncurls his angry mane. Dryden.
To become uncurled, or straight.
Not current. Specifically: Not passing in common payment; not receivable at par or full value; as, uncurrent notes. Shak.
To free from a curse or an execration. Shak.
To remove a curtain from; to reveal. Moore.
A hook or claw.
Not customable, or subject to custom duties.
Uncustomable; also, not having paid duty or customs. Smollett.
Not cut; not separated or divided by cutting or otherwise; -- said especially of books, periodicals, and the like, when the leaves have not been separated by trimming in binding.
Not ground, or otherwise cut, into a certain shape; as, an uncut diamond. Uncut velvet,a fabric woven like velvet, but with the loops of the warp threads uncut.
Unknown; strange. [Obs.] -- n.
A stranger. [Obs.]
A fabric woven like velvet, but with the loops of the warp threads uncut.
See Uncipher.
